newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spanish markets recoil as funds flow north.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spanish markets recoil as funds flow north.

text.p: Spanish financial markets recoiled on Friday as investors took fright over recent dramatic gains and fled to mainstream markets to the north, but analysts are confident a more moderate rally will follow.

A wave of euphoria that Spain would join the launch of European monetary union fuelled a buying frenzy in recent months which has propelled the stock and bond markets to record highs and fed a strong appreciation of the peseta.
But economists said that markets might have jumped the gun, discounting huge interest rate cuts and minimal inflation rates, and were now taking a well-deserved breather.

"Some foreign investors have thought the rally in the short term is exhausted and other markets appear more attractive in terms of price," said Valentin Fernandez, analyst at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
"But it's not a turning point, the trend continues to be positive and fundamentally nothing has changed with inflation and interest rates still on a downward trend," he added.
The stock market fell 1.4 percent on Friday as nervous investors got out and bond prices also dropped.
Analysts said in the short term they expected to see further losses as markets prepared for the next stage of the rally.

"Technically the markets are very overbought and logically they need a rest before the rally returns, but it's difficult to think that the rally will continue as strongly as before," said one analyst.
In the bond market, the 10-year benchmark bond future slipped 25 ticks to trade at 113.63 by 1200 GMT, after hitting an all-time high earlier in the week of 114.98.
The yield spread of 10-year Spanish bonos to German Bunds -- a reflection of how risky the market regards Spanish bonds to be -- widened to 94 basis points (bp) from a low of 83 bp on Wednesday.
The spread has narrowed from 330 bp since last March on the belief Spain will be among the first to join the single European currency in 1999, by which time the spread must narrow to zero.
"At a spread of around 85 bp the market is discounting a lot of good things and is discounting the almost 100 percent possibility that Spain will be in EMU," said Fernandez.
Many analysts said they expected the spread to narrow to around 50 bp by the end of the year as the rally returned.
In the stock market, the Ibex-35 index of leading shares tumbled 77.03 points or 1.41 percent to 5,373.71 on Friday, after hitting 5,571 earlier in the year.
In the currency markets, the peseta sprung back through the key 84.00 per mark level, broken earlier in January, and analysts expect it to hover around these levels for some time.
"Over the next few months the dollar will come roaring back and we'll see the peseta move back to below 84.00 again," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
"But the Bank of Spain will use both weapons (intervention and rate cuts) to curb the strength," he added.
By 1200 GMT, the peseta was trading at 84.30 per mark.
Many analysts expect the bond and equity markets to rally in the medium term but some were less optimistic in the long run.

"There will be no more monetary easing left to do by the end of 1997 and concerns about inflation in 1998 could appear from energy and raw material prices or simply inflation bottoming," said Lumholdt.
"You have a cocktail for expectations to change quite dramatically in Spain and it could get very bearish," he added.
In the meantime, however, analysts said EMU expectations had not yet been shattered, although they expected Spanish markets to underperform the bigger markets in the near future.

"I don't think expectations about EMU have been shattered and the market is still optimistic, but that isn't to say that there won't be a shake-up later on down the road," said an analyst at a Spanish bank.
